title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.1.1 How did Statistical Quality Control begin?
key_findings: Shewhart memo with sketch of a modern control chart dated 16 May 1924 (Bell Labs).
Shewhart 1931 book Economic Control of Quality of Manufactured Product (Van Nostrand).
Dodge and Romig applied statistics to sampling inspection; medieval guilds relied on apprenticeship.
practical_applications: History timeline for QA training; separates process control from inspection.
limitations: Short overview; no WWII/Deming coverage on this page.

title: Economic Control of Quality of Manufactured Product
key_findings: Introduced control charts and the distinction between chance (common) and assignable (special) causes of variation (per NIST handbook and secondary summaries).
practical_applications: Do not react to a single bad post/clip as if it were a special cause; look for patterns first.
limitations: Book not read; content from secondary sources.

title: Out of the Crisis (14 points for management)
key_findings: Point 3: cease dependence on inspection to achieve quality; build quality in from the start (wording consistent across quoted editions, 1982 MIT CAES / 1986).
Deming Institute: the 14 points are not meant to be applied as a stand-alone checklist.
practical_applications: Prevent defects with briefs, validators and templates rather than only final review.
limitations: Edition year differs between sources (1982 vs 1986); book not read; Deming Institute page returned 403.

title: The Quality Trilogy
key_findings: Quality Progress 19(8):19-24; quality planning, quality control, quality improvement as a continuing cycle (per ASQ record and secondary summaries).
practical_applications: Map studio QA to plan (criteria) / control (checks) / improve (lessons log).
limitations: Full text not read.

title: Quality management principles (ISO 9000 family)
key_findings: Seven principles: customer focus, leadership, engagement of people, process approach, improvement, evidence-based decision making, relationship management (per search results quoting ISO brochure).
Search results suggest ISO 9001:2026 / ISO 9000:2026 editions now exist; status of 2015 edition unconfirmed.
practical_applications: Evidence-based decision making as a house principle for creative QC.
limitations: iso.org returned 403; content from search summary only.

title: The Art of Software Testing
key_findings: Defines testing as 'the process of executing a program with the intent of finding errors'; a successful test is one that finds an error (per O'Reilly excerpt and secondary sources).
practical_applications: Critic role is to make the work fail, not to reassure the maker.
limitations: Read only via search excerpts; one source misdates to 1977.

title: The ML Test Score: A Rubric for ML Production Readiness and Technical Debt Reduction
authors: Eric Breck, Shanqing Cai, Eric Nielsen, Michael Salib, D. Sculley
key_findings: 28 specific tests and monitoring needs for production ML systems, drawn from Google experience.
Model prediction behaviour is hard to specify a priori, so tests and monitoring must be designed explicitly.
practical_applications: Golden-set and regression testing for AI-driven creative pipelines (data, prompt/model, tools, post-release monitoring).
limitations: Practitioner experience paper; scoring details only from secondary source.

title: A coefficient of agreement for nominal scales
key_findings: Introduced kappa: chance-corrected agreement between two raters on nominal categories (Educational and Psychological Measurement 20:37-46).
practical_applications: Pass/fail agreement between two reviewers.
limitations: Not read; limited to two raters and nominal data (per Hayes & Krippendorff).

title: The measurement of observer agreement for categorical data
authors: J. Richard Landis, Gary G. Koch
key_findings: General statistical methodology for multivariate categorical observer-reliability data; generalized kappa-type statistics and tests for interobserver bias (abstract).
Best known for kappa interpretation bands in 0.20 steps; secondary sources note the bands rest on opinion, not evidence.
practical_applications: Use bands only as shared vocabulary, not as pass thresholds.
limitations: Bands are conventional; full text not read.

title: Intraclass correlations: Uses in assessing rater reliability
authors: Patrick E. Shrout, Joseph L. Fleiss
key_findings: Guidelines for choosing among six ICC forms for n targets rated by k judges; choice depends on statistical model and intended use; confidence intervals reviewed (abstract).
practical_applications: Pick ICC form for continuous 0-100 quality scores.
limitations: Abstract only.

title: High agreement but low kappa: I. The problems of two paradoxes (and II. Resolving the paradoxes)
authors: Alvan R. Feinstein, Domenic V. Cicchetti
key_findings: Kappa can be low despite high observed agreement when marginals are imbalanced; asymmetric imbalance can yield higher kappa than balanced.
Part II proposes reporting separate positive and negative agreement indices (p_pos, p_neg) alongside kappa.
practical_applications: When almost all items pass, report p_pos/p_neg or alpha instead of kappa alone.
limitations: Only search summaries read.

title: Answering the call for a standard reliability measure for coding data
key_findings: Five criteria for a good reliability index: any number of independent observers, grounded in categories actually used, meaningful 0/1 scale points, appropriate to level of measurement, known sampling behaviour.
Percent agreement fails most criteria; Cohen's kappa defines zero as statistical independence of observers and can be inflated by systematic disagreement; Scott's pi limited to two coders/nominal.
Krippendorff's alpha satisfies all; works for nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio, any number of observers, missing data; bootstrap CI and probability of falling below alpha_min.
Worked example: nominal alpha 0.4765 vs ordinal 0.7598 on the same data; 95% CI 0.708-0.808; q=0.9473 of failing alpha_min 0.80 vs q=0.0125 for 0.70.
practical_applications: Studio standard: ordinal Krippendorff's alpha with bootstrap CI for rubric pilots.
limitations: Communication/content-analysis context; macro tooling dated.

title: A Guideline of Selecting and Reporting Intraclass Correlation Coefficients for Reliability Research
authors: Terry K. Koo, Mae Y. Li
key_findings: ICC forms defined by model (one-way random, two-way random, two-way mixed), type (single vs mean of k), definition (consistency vs absolute agreement).
Report software, model, type, definition, estimate and 95% CI.
Cutoffs: <0.5 poor, 0.5-0.75 moderate, 0.75-0.9 good, >0.9 excellent, judged on the 95% CI not the point estimate.
Aim for at least 30 heterogeneous samples and at least 3 raters; low ICC can come from low between-subject variability.
practical_applications: Reporting template for continuous quality scores.
limitations: Clinical-research guideline; cutoffs conventional.

title: Updated guidelines on selecting an intraclass correlation coefficient for interrater reliability, with applications to incomplete observational designs
authors: Debby ten Hove, Terrence D. Jorgensen, L. Andries van der Ark
key_findings: Existing ICC guidelines ignore incomplete designs, lack a coherent account of error variance, and misunderstand fixed vs random raters.
Generalizability-theory based guidelines; raters should seldom if ever be considered fixed; flowchart of four choices.
practical_applications: When raters differ across items, use G-theory ICC guidance.
limitations: Abstract only; online 2022, issue 2024.

title: Validity of psychological assessment: Validation of inferences from persons' responses and performances as scientific inquiry into score meaning
key_findings: Traditional content/criterion/construct split is fragmented; unified construct validity covers score meaning, value implications and social consequences of score use.
Six aspects: content, substantive, structural, generalizability, external, consequential (abstract and secondary sources).
practical_applications: Check that a creative rubric measures the intended construct and consider side effects of using it.
limitations: Abstract only; threats terminology from general knowledge of the article.

title: The use of scoring rubrics: Reliability, validity and educational consequences
key_findings: Per citing papers: rubric studies focused mostly on reliability; rubrics may enhance reliable scoring, but a rubric alone does not guarantee reliability or validity.
practical_applications: Pilot rubrics and measure agreement before relying on them.
limitations: Neither abstract nor full text read; findings via secondary descriptions.

title: Appropriate Criteria: Key to Effective Rubrics
key_findings: A rubric = criteria + performance level descriptions; checklists and rating scales lack the latter.
Analytic rubrics score criteria one at a time (better for feedback); holistic give one judgement (faster).
Generality is 'perhaps the most important characteristic'; descriptive level language helps learners more than evaluative.
Higher-education rubrics 2005-2017 mostly analytic with 4-5 levels; no discernible pattern between rubric type and reliability/validity.
Compliance criteria ('has three sources') misdirect effort and mis-measure learning.
practical_applications: Write observable descriptors; separate checks from quality criteria.
limitations: Education context; ~87% of page read.

title: Response style and cross-cultural comparisons of rating scales among East Asian and North American students
authors: Chuansheng Chen, Shin-ying Lee, Harold W. Stevenson
key_findings: Japanese and Chinese (Taiwan) students used scale midpoints more; US students used extremes more (57 seven-point Likert items, about 5,000 students).
Individualism related to extreme responding; differences small and generally did not alter comparisons of item means.
practical_applications: Consider forced-choice or even-numbered scales when collecting Thai/Asian ratings.
limitations: Not Thai data; abstract only.

title: Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments: A Practical Guide to A/B Testing
authors: Ron Kohavi, Diane Tang, Ya Xu
key_findings: Covers OEC definition, trustworthiness checks and a chapter 'Twyman's Law and Experimentation Trustworthiness' (any figure that looks interesting or different is usually wrong).
Authors drew on companies each running 20,000+ controlled experiments a year (publisher blurb).
practical_applications: Pre-register the OEC; distrust surprising wins until the pipeline is checked.
limitations: Publisher pages only; Twyman 'usually wrong' is a heuristic, not a measured rate.

title: Controlled experiments on the web: survey and practical guide
authors: Ron Kohavi, Roger Longbotham, Dan Sommerfield, Randal M. Henne
key_findings: Controlled experiments are the best scientific design for establishing causality of a change on user behaviour; listen to customers, not the HiPPO.
OEC defined in advance; A/A (null) tests validate the system; robots can skew results.
Minimum sample size per variant at 95% confidence / 80% power: n = 16 sigma^2 / Delta^2 (from van Belle).
Limitations: no 'why', short-term vs long-term, primacy and newness effects, features must be implemented, consistency, launch events.
practical_applications: Power calculation before ad split tests; run tests for multiple weeks when novelty is likely.
limitations: Large-traffic web context; formula symbols garbled in text extraction (standard form stated).

title: Online Experimentation at Microsoft (ThinkWeek paper, public version)
authors: Ron Kohavi, Thomas Crook, Roger Longbotham, Brian Frasca, Randy Henne, Juan Lavista Ferres, Tamir Melamed
key_findings: ExP estimate: of ideas tested, about 1/3 good, 1/3 flat, 1/3 negative; ideas thought good that hurt metrics are about one third of experiments.
Failed A/A tests revealed bugs (page cache key, cookie assignment) that biased experiments.
HiPPO awareness campaign; OEC should favour long-term value.
practical_applications: Validate the evaluation system (A/A, golden set) before trusting it; expect many ideas to fail.
limitations: Internal company estimates; not peer-reviewed.

title: Diagnosing Sample Ratio Mismatch in Online Controlled Experiments: A Taxonomy and Rules of Thumb for Practitioners
authors: Aleksander Fabijan, Jayant Gupchup, Somit Gupta, Jeff Omhover, Wen Qin, Lukas Vermeer, Pavel Dmitriev
key_findings: SRM = observed sample ratio differs from expected; a symptom of many data-quality issues, like a fever.
Ignoring SRM without root cause can make a bad change look good; taxonomy of causes by experiment stage.
practical_applications: Check that ad split tests deliver the intended split before reading results.
limitations: Abstract only.

title: Power failure: why small sample size undermines the reliability of neuroscience
authors: Katherine S. Button, John P. A. Ioannidis, Claire Mokrysz, Brian A. Nosek, Jonathan Flint, Emma S. J. Robinson, Marcus R. Munafo
key_findings: Median statistical power in neuroscience about 21% (about 8-31% by subfield).
Low power reduces chance of detecting true effects, lowers positive predictive value, and inflates effect estimates (winner's curse).
practical_applications: Treat small-sample A/B wins as hypotheses; replicate.
limitations: Later reanalysis argued power varies widely by subfield (per critiques in search results).

title: Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs for Generalized Causal Inference
authors: William R. Shadish, Thomas D. Cook, Donald T. Campbell
key_findings: Standard taxonomy of validity threats; history, maturation, regression, testing and instrumentation are especially relevant to pre-post designs without comparison (per secondary sources).
practical_applications: Design before/after benchmarks with blinding, held-out tasks and concurrent baselines.
limitations: Book not read.

title: Vanity Metrics vs. Actionable Metrics (guest post)
key_findings: Vanity metrics make you feel good but give no clear guidance; actionable metrics show clear cause and effect.
Use split tests, per-customer/segment metrics, cohort and funnel analysis; 'the key to actionable metrics is having as few as possible'.
practical_applications: Judge shop content by chats/appointments by cohort, not likes.
limitations: Practitioner opinion; vanity metrics can be leading indicators.

title: 'Improving ratings': audit in the British University system
key_findings: 'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure' (generalising Goodhart's law via Hoskin).
Audit has a life of its own; 'Measurement and target rise together'; expected grades lose power to discriminate.
practical_applications: Separate scorers from beneficiaries of scores; refresh golden sets to avoid overfitting.
limitations: Anthropological essay, not quantitative; Campbell's law may have priority.

title: ITU-T P.800 (08/96) Methods for subjective determination of transmission quality
key_findings: In force; approved 30 Aug 1996; methods and procedures for subjective evaluation of transmission quality; this version added an annex on Comparison Category Rating (CCR).
practical_applications: Basis for ACR-style listening tests of TTS lines.
limitations: Only catalogue/summary pages read; ACR 5-point details not verified this session.

title: ITU-T P.808 (06/2021) Subjective evaluation of speech quality with a crowdsourcing approach
key_findings: Crowdsourcing approach where participants rate speech in their own environments; complements lab methods in P.800 and P.835; annex on ACR listening tests (summary).
practical_applications: Run cheap listener panels with qualification and quality control.
limitations: Summary only.

title: An Open Source Implementation of ITU-T Recommendation P.808 with Validation
key_findings: Open-source P.808 on Mechanical Turk incl. ACR, DCR, CCR; qualification merged into rating task.
Validated against lab P.800 MOS and assessed reproducibility; quantified impact of environment tests, gold and trapping questions, rating-pattern checks, headset test.
practical_applications: Gold/trap questions in listener forms for TTS.
limitations: Abstract only; correlation numbers not read; preprint.

title: Recommendation ITU-R BT.500-15 (05/2023) Methodologies for the subjective assessment of the quality of television images
key_findings: In force since 2023-05; methods incl. DSCQS, SSCQE, SDSCE, SAMVIQ; lab and home viewing environments; quality vs impairment assessments.
Objective measurement alone may not fully characterise system performance; subjective tests supplement it.
practical_applications: Rationale for human panels when judging images/video.
limitations: Search summary only.

title: Image quality assessment: from error visibility to structural similarity
authors: Zhou Wang, Alan C. Bovik, Hamid R. Sheikh, Eero P. Simoncelli
key_findings: Proposes SSIM, a full-reference measure of degradation of structural information, compared with subjective ratings on a JPEG/JPEG2000 database.
practical_applications: Check export/compression damage against the master; not an aesthetic score.
limitations: Needs a reference image; abstract only.

title: Rethinking FID: Towards a Better Evaluation Metric for Image Generation
key_findings: FID's Inception features poorly represent modern T2I content, rely on a normality assumption, need many samples, contradict human raters, miss gradual improvements and distortion levels.
Proposes CMMD (CLIP embeddings + MMD, RBF kernel).
practical_applications: Never judge single generated images with FID; validate any metric against human ratings.
limitations: Authors propose a competing metric; abstract only.

title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
key_findings: GPT-4 judge agreement with experts 85% excluding ties (human-human 81%); 66% vs 63% including ties.

Position consistency on swap: GPT-4 65.0%, GPT-3.5 46.2%, Claude-v1 23.8%; repetitive-list verbosity attack fooled Claude-v1 and GPT-3.5 91.3%, GPT-4 8.7%; self-enhancement about 10% (GPT-4), 25% (Claude-v1) with limited data.
Mitigations: swap positions and count only consistent wins, few-shot (65% to 77.5% consistency), reference-guided grading (math failures 70% to 15%); chain-of-thought helped less.
practical_applications: Run AI critics pairwise twice with swapped order and with references (brief, product photo).
limitations: Single study, English chat helpfulness; judged models now outdated.

title: All That's 'Human' Is Not Gold: Evaluating Human Evaluation of Generated Text
authors: Elizabeth Clark, Tal August, Sofia Serrano, Nikita Haduong, Suchin Gururangan, Noah A. Smith
key_findings: Untrained evaluators distinguished GPT-3 from human text (stories, news, recipes) at about chance.
Three training methods raised accuracy to about 55%, not significant; raters gave contradictory reasons.
practical_applications: Use lay viewers for preference/comprehension, not technical authenticity judgements.
limitations: English text, GPT-2/3 era; abstract only.

title: Human evaluation of automatically generated text: Current trends and best practice guidelines
authors: Chris van der Lee, Albert Gatt, Emiel van Miltenburg, Emiel Krahmer
key_findings: Little agreement on how NLG should be evaluated; high variation in human evaluation practice.
Best practices linked to planning stage and execution & release stage.
practical_applications: Plan human evaluations of captions/scripts in advance: criteria, scale, raters, agreement reporting.
limitations: Abstract only.
license: open access per OpenAlex (licence not checked)

title: Recommendation ITU-R BS.1770-5: Algorithms to measure audio programme loudness and true-peak audio level
key_findings: Current version BS.1770-5, approved 11/2023, in force.
Defines programme loudness (LKFS = LUFS) and true-peak measurement (per existing registry entry).
practical_applications: Measure every clip's integrated loudness and true peak with a BS.1770 meter (ffmpeg ebur128/loudnorm).
limitations: Status page only this session.

title: EBU R 128: Loudness normalisation and permitted maximum level of audio signals
key_findings: Target -23 LUFS programme loudness; tolerance tightened to +/-0.5 LU in v3.0 (June 2014).
Publication page shows v5.0 dated 21 Nov 2023 (adds cinematic-content reference).
Max true peak -1 dBTP (from registry record of v4.0 full text read earlier).
practical_applications: Broadcast reference point; social targets differ.
limitations: Page did not show the true-peak number; key reused from SOURCE_REGISTRY (v4.0, 2020).

title: Loudness normalization on Spotify (Spotify for Artists support)
key_findings: Default normalisation -14 LUFS (Normal); Premium Loud -11, Quiet -19; measured per ITU 1770.
Keep true peak below -1 dBTP for lossy formats; below -2 dBTP if master is louder than -14 LUFS.
practical_applications: External justification for the studio's -14 LUFS social target.
limitations: Spotify only; not IG/TikTok/YouTube.

title: A surgical safety checklist to reduce morbidity and mortality in a global population
authors: Alex B. Haynes, Thomas G. Weiser, William R. Berry, Stuart R. Lipsitz, et al.
key_findings: 8 hospitals in 8 cities (WHO Safe Surgery Saves Lives), 3,733 patients before vs 3,955 after a 19-item checklist.
Death 1.5% to 0.8% (P=0.003); inpatient complications 11.0% to 7.0% (P<0.001); 'associated with' reductions.
practical_applications: Short checklists at natural pause points (sign-in, time-out, sign-out).
limitations: Pre-post without concurrent control; Hawthorne and secular trends possible.

title: Introduction of surgical safety checklists in Ontario, Canada
authors: David R. Urbach, Anand Govindarajan, Refik Saskin, Andrew S. Wilton, Nancy N. Baxter
key_findings: Natural experiment: 101 hospitals, 109,341 procedures before vs 106,370 after checklist adoption.
Mortality 0.71% to 0.65% (OR 0.91, 95% CI 0.80-1.03, P=0.13); complications 3.86% to 3.82% (OR 0.97, P=0.29); no significant reduction.
practical_applications: Mandated checklists without local adaptation may become ritual; evaluate QA tools with controls.
limitations: Administrative data; 3-month windows.

title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of the effect of the World Health Organization surgical safety checklist on postoperative complications
authors: J. Bergs, J. Hellings, I. Cleemput, O. Zurel, V. De Troyer, M. Van Hiel, J.-L. Demeere, D. Claeys, D. Vandijck
key_findings: 7 of 723 studies included; marked methodological heterogeneity.
RR any complication 0.59 (0.47-0.74), mortality 0.77 (0.60-0.98), SSI 0.57 (0.41-0.79); effect correlated with adherence (Q=0.82, P=0.042).
Evidence 'highly suggestive' but not definitive without higher-quality studies.
practical_applications: Checklist effect depends on adherence to the embedded care steps.
limitations: Mostly observational primary studies.

title: Postoperative Adverse Events Inconsistently Improved by the World Health Organization Surgical Safety Checklist: A Systematic Literature Review of 25 Studies
authors: Elzerie de Jager, Chris McKenna, Lynne Bartlett, Ronny Gunnarsson, Yik-Hong Ho
key_findings: 25 studies (2 RCTs, 13 prospective, 10 retrospective); no meta-analysis because pooling heterogeneous observational studies may be biased.
Only 4 had concurrent controls; many underpowered; teamwork training confounded; effects inconsistent; mortality decreased in no developed-nation study but in 75% of developing-nation studies.
Positive changes may reflect temporal changes, confounding and publication bias.
practical_applications: Before/after QA claims need concurrent controls.
limitations: Abstract only.

title: Safety of surgery: quality assessment of meta-analyses on the WHO checklist
key_findings: Three meta-analyses rated with AMSTAR 2: all associated the checklist with lower complications/mortality, but overall confidence was critically low (mostly observational, biased studies).
practical_applications: Distinguish 'many studies agree' from 'strong evidence'.
limitations: Single author; abstract only.

title: An intervention to decrease catheter-related bloodstream infections in the ICU
authors: Peter Pronovost, Dale Needham, Sean Berenholtz, et al.
key_findings: 108 ICUs agreed, 103 reported; 375,757 catheter-days; median CRBSI per 1000 catheter-days 2.7 to 0 at 3 months; mean 7.7 to 1.4 at 16-18 months; IRR 0.62 to 0.34; up to 66% sustained reduction.
practical_applications: Combined checklist + data feedback + team authority as a QA system.
limitations: Collaborative cohort, no randomised control.

title: Explaining Michigan: Developing an Ex Post Theory of a Quality Improvement Program
authors: Mary Dixon-Woods, Charles L. Bosk, Emma Louise Aveling, Christine A. Goeschel, Peter J. Pronovost
key_findings: Michigan success came from a complex social intervention, not a 'simple checklist': isomorphic pressure, networked community, reframing the problem, multiple interventions, infection data as disciplinary force, 'hard edges' (e.g. nurses empowered to challenge doctors).
Copying surface features risks 'cargo cult' imitation; data discipline depends on legitimacy; gaming/underreporting is a risk.
practical_applications: Give the studio critic real stop authority; build QA as a team practice, not paperwork.
limitations: Ex post theory from insiders + social scientists; about 73% of page read.

title: The Checklist Manifesto: How to Get Things Right
key_findings: Distinguishes DO-CONFIRM (work from memory, then pause to confirm) and READ-DO (do each step as read) checklists, from Boeing's Dan Boorman; WHO surgical checklist used DO-CONFIRM (per secondary summaries).
practical_applications: Use DO-CONFIRM at studio pause points; READ-DO for rare complex setups.
limitations: Book not read; secondary summaries only; popular non-fiction.
